name: strops-split
algorithm: Split a 50 MB text at "e" with each language's std splitter (empty pieces kept), trim each piece, and iterate its whitespace-separated words; the piece count, an FNV-1a over the trimmed lengths and the word lengths, wrapping; rounds times (README.md).

skip.c: no std split in C (strtok writes its input and is not reentrant)
skip.mk-wrap: the checksum already uses the wrapping operators; splitting has no arithmetic to wrap

no_counts: B24 does not apply: an idiomatic row compares libraries; every splitter keeps empty pieces and every trim and word iterator strips the same ASCII bytes of this text, so the checksum checks every result
notes: Iterators named: mk str.Split, str.Trim, str.Words; rust str::split(char), str::trim, str::split_whitespace; zig std.mem.splitScalar, std.mem.trim (an ASCII set), std.mem.tokenizeAny; go strings.SplitSeq, strings.TrimSpace, strings.FieldsSeq; cs MemoryExtensions.Split, ReadOnlySpan<char>.Trim, MemoryExtensions.SplitAny(SearchValues<char>). Mk, Rust and Go trim and split words at whitespace, Zig and C# split words at an ASCII whitespace set; the text is ASCII letters, spaces and newlines, so all strip the same bytes.
The input is wordfreq's file (the same data spec, so one generated file serves both rows).
